MeshLink routing simulation — stage B: how should messages find their way?

Every number on this page is simulated. It comes from a simplified computer model of phones and Bluetooth links, calibrated against a few lab measurements. It is not a measurement on real devices.

The question

Stage A settled which phones connect to each other (N1+N2 “diverse views”, at most d = 5 live links per phone). Stage B asks how a message then travels across that mesh, hop by hop, to one recipient (unicast) or to everyone (mesh broadcast). Each option trades traffic for reliability and speed:

  • U1 managed flood: every phone passes every message on to all its links. No route knowledge needed; very robust, but every message costs a transmission on nearly every link of the mesh.
  • U2 scoped topology + source route: phones announce their neighbors up to 3 hops away; if the sender knows a path it sends along it, otherwise it floods (as in a deployed phone chat app).
  • U3 Babel-like distance vector: every phone keeps a table “to reach X, send to neighbor Y” and keeps it fresh with periodic and triggered updates (the routing-template choice).
  • U4 on-demand (AODV-like): a phone looks for a route only when it has something to send, with a search that widens ring by ring; nothing is sent while the mesh is idle.

For mesh broadcast: B1 flood, B2 fanout subset (relays forward to only about log₂(links) links), B3 Plumtree (payload along a self-repairing tree, short “I have it” notes on the other links) and gossipsub (the libp2p publish/subscribe protocol, scaled to BLE link counts).

Messages carry a message lifetime. Following the accepted design: no phone forwards or holds an expired message, and a phone takes a message into store-and-forward (holding it until a route appears) only if at least the minimum hold time of lifetime is left. Phones’ clocks may be off by up to ±30 s. Recipients are addressed by a routing tag that can rotate every 15 minutes for privacy.

Each setting was run with several random seeds; tables show the mean and a 95% confidence interval (±). Unless stated otherwise: lifetime 5 min, minimum hold 10 s, clock skew ±30 s, rotation off. Every simulated run lasts 15 minutes; the first 2 minutes are warm-up and not measured. Traffic: every phone sends a chat message every 4 minutes on average (to two nearby contacts and one far one), and some phone sends a mesh broadcast every 15 s.

1500 simulation runs (12500 protocol results; all protocols of one run share the same simulated phones, movements and links, so they face exactly the same conditions).

What we found

Every number below comes from the simulator. None of them is a device measurement. "Delivery" counts only messages whose recipient was online and reachable when they were sent. "Max load" is the busiest phone's average send rate.

Unicast: one phone to another

  • Low density: no protocol meets the 99% delivery target in every cell. This includes plain flooding (U1). U1 passes 30 of 36 cells (mean 99.55%, worst 98.4%). U3 passes 29 of 32 (mean 99.76%). U4 passes 25 of 36 (mean 98.98%, worst 95.7%). U2 passes 18 of 36. The failing cells are mostly corridor (chain) cells, cells with half the phones on iOS, and N=1000 static. In those cells the network keeps splitting and rejoining, so even flooding misses.
  • Medium density: U1 and U3 pass every cell. Ranked by max load: U1 is first at 3,206 B/s and U3 second at 3,968 B/s. U2 fails 1 cell (98.92%). U4 fails 3 delivery cells and 4 first-message cells.
  • High density: all four pass. Ranked by max load: U4 (380 B/s, p95 2.2 s), U2, U1, U3.
  • Cost differs by about 10×. At N=1000, medium density, a flood (U1) costs the busiest phone about 12.8 KB/s. U4 costs about 0.8 KB/s. U4 also sends no idle control traffic. The price is latency: U4's p95 latency is 9.5 s (low), 2.9 s (medium) and 2.2 s (high). The floods stay around 0.4–0.5 s.
  • U3 (distance-vector) idle traffic stays under the 10% ceiling: at most 8.5% in a cell, N=200, high density. It grows with N and density: 0.5% at N=50 low, 7.3% at N=200 high. At N=1000 the simulator could not finish a U3 run, so U3 is not shown at N=1000. Treat U3 as unsafe to scale until a cheaper variant is tested.
  • Verdict: ambiguous. No unicast protocol meets every criterion in every density class. U1 is the most reliable but costs the most. U4 is cheapest but slow, and it misses the first-message limit in some half-iOS cells. Stage C should test a hybrid (U6: route when a route is known, otherwise hold or flood with a limited scope). It should also test U4 with tuned store-and-forward.

Mesh broadcast: one phone to everyone

  • Low density: no protocol passes every cell. B1 (flood) is the most robust: 32 of 36 cells, mean 99.44%. B3 (Plumtree) passes 26 of 36 and gossipsub 15 of 36. B2 (probabilistic) falls off a coverage cliff, with a worst cell of 62%.
  • Medium and high density: gossipsub, B3 and B1 pass every cell, ranked in that order by max load (about 45, 48 and 72 B/s at medium). B1 has the lowest p95 latency (245 ms vs 424 ms for gossipsub at medium).

First message to a new destination (p95, destinations at most 3 hops away)

U1 and U2 pass in every cell. U3 passes in all but one low-density cell. U4 misses in 1 low-density and 4 medium-density cells, all with half the phones on iOS. In those cells the worst p95 is 15–18 s, with very wide confidence intervals: a few runs waited for a backgrounded iOS phone to wake. The 1 s (classical) / 1.5 s (post-quantum) targets are met when the path does not include a sleeping iOS phone.

Message lifetime and store-and-forward

  • ±30 s clock skew with a 30 s lifetime does not work. Delivery falls to 55–87%, depending on protocol and mobility. Without skew, a 30 s lifetime is fine (U1 99.8%, U4 98.4–99.7%). With lifetime ≥ 5 min, skew has no measurable effect. Lifetimes must be well above the skew bound.
  • The minimum hold time matters only at a 30 s lifetime. There it refuses 3–7% of store-and-forward takes for U4, without changing delivery. For U3 with a 60 s hold, it refuses 8–21% and costs up to about 6 pp of delivery. At lifetimes ≥ 5 min the hold time has no measurable effect.
  • The 1 h and 24 h lifetimes behave the same as 5 min, because a run lasts only 15 simulated minutes. That is a model limit, not a finding.

Routing-tag rotation every 15 minutes

Measured as paired per-run differences. Averaged per density class, every protocol stays within the budget (≤ +10% bytes sent, ≤ 1 pp delivery lost). Two single cells exceed it: U2 +11.2% bytes in one medium cell, and U3 −1.75 pp (low) and −1.31 pp (medium) delivery in its worst cells. U4 is the least affected (≤ +3.3% bytes, about 0 pp delivery).

Bridge variant: prefer a newly discovered phone from another group

  • After two groups meet, the first link between them forms faster with the bridge variant in every cell. Examples: low N=200 half-iOS 6.5 → 1.7 s, medium N=200 Android-only 11.9 → 3.4 s, high N=1000 20.8 → 5.6 s.
  • Time until the largest group has rejoined:
    • medium and high density: 2–3.5× faster (e.g. high N=200 26.0 → 6.5 s);
    • low density, Android-only: modestly faster (10.2 → 6.7 s at N=50);
    • low density, half-iOS, N=200/1000: no clear effect (confidence intervals overlap).
    At low density, sleeping iOS phones dominate the delay, not link choice.
  • Cost: in mobile scenarios at medium and high density, link-ups per phone-minute rise 40–60% (e.g. medium walking 9.6 → 14.3). Static scenarios rise only about 5%. Control traffic rises about 5–15%. The largest-group fraction does not get worse.
  • With traffic (low density, N=200, merge), delivery differences are within the confidence intervals.
  • Verdict: adopt it for merge repair, but add a rate limit, because the extra link churn in moving crowds is real.

What was cut

N=1000 used static mobility only, ran without U3, and used 5 seeds. N=50 and N=200 ran the full requested grid with 10 seeds. The full reasons are in the run notes at the end of the report.

Decision criteria scoreboard

Criteria from the ticket, checked in every cell (one cell = density × mesh size × movement × platform mix × d). A protocol passes a cell if (1) it delivers ≥ 99% of messages at low and medium density and ≥ 95% at high density (counting messages whose recipient was in the sender’s connected group when sent), (2) its idle control traffic (route upkeep that runs even with no messages) uses ≤ 10% of link capacity, and (3) the first message to a new contact arrives within 1 s (95th percentile) for classical and 1.5 s for post-quantum encryption, for recipients ≤ 3 hops away. Among protocols that pass, the ranking is: lowest maximum load on any single phone, then lowest 95th-percentile delay. Delivery uses the cell mean over seeds.

Routing-tag rotation every 15 minutes

Recipients are addressed by a routing tag that changes every 15 minutes. Old routes then point at a tag nobody uses any more, so routes must be found again. Budget from the ticket: at most +10% transmissions and at most −1 percentage point delivery. Each run carries both variants over identical links and traffic, so the differences below are paired per run (mean ± 95% CI over all runs of that density, and the worst cell mean). Transmissions = all link sends of data and control packets, counted as bytes sent. U1 does not use routes and is unaffected.

Message lifetime, minimum hold time and clock skew

Rules under test: never forward or hold an expired message; take a message into store-and-forward only if at least the minimum hold time of its lifetime is left. Swept on N = 200, low and medium density, static and walking, Android only, d = 5, rotation on: lifetime 30 s / 5 min / 1 h / 24 h × minimum hold 0 / 10 / 60 s × clock skew 0 / ±30 s for U1 and U4; U3 only at lifetime 30 s and 5 min with skew ±30 s (cost). A simulated run lasts 15 minutes, so 1 h and 24 h lifetimes never expire inside a run: those rows show the “holds until a route appears” limit, not long-term storage behavior.

Variant: N1+N2 plus “prefer a newly discovered phone from another group” (bridge)

When two groups of phones that had been apart come into radio range, plain N1+N2 may keep all its links inside its own group. The bridge variant notices a phone it has just started hearing (silent for ≥ 60 s, first heard within the last 10 s) that is not reachable within 2 hops, and connects to it, if necessary by dropping its most redundant link. Measured in the partition-and-merge scenario (two groups apart for a while, then merging) without message traffic: time until the first link between the groups, and time until the largest connected group recovers. Lower is better.

Words used here

  • node / phone: one device running MeshLink. peer: another node in radio range. link: a live BLE connection.
  • hop: one link a message crosses. hop limit: the most hops a message may travel.
  • message lifetime: how long a message stays valid; afterwards nobody forwards or holds it.
  • store-and-forward: a node holds a message while no route exists and sends it once one appears.
  • minimum hold time: a node takes a message into store-and-forward only if at least this much lifetime is left.
  • routing tag: the 8-byte address a message is routed to; it can rotate every 15 minutes.
  • 95% CI (±): range that would contain the true simulated mean in 95% of repetitions with new seeds.
